numerical_failure.observed_behavior: For `skipna=False`, `DataFrame.median` can discard the imaginary part of complex results depending on column order: `df.median(skipna=False)["b"]` returns `2.0` instead of the complex value `2+3j`.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: `DataFrame.median(skipna=False)` should return a missing value that carries the data’s own dtype; for the shown data it should preserve the complex imaginary part so that `df.median(skipna=False)["b"]` returns `2+3j` (and column reordering should not change the complex median result for `"b"`).
trigger_conditions: Calling `median(skipna=False)` on a 2-D `DataFrame` where one column causes a missing-value short-circuit (`nanmedian` `skipna=False` short-circuit returns a bare `np.nan`).

Column order affects the output dtype for the 2-D path: the 2-D implementation builds the result using `np.apply_along_axis`, taking output dtype from the first slice, so a missing-value column that appears first casts later columns down to `float64` and discards the imaginary part of complex columns.
At least one column includes `np.nan` alongside complex values where the median for the non-missing column is well-defined (as in the reproducer).

input_output_examples.source: PR#68487 reproducer snippet: `df.median(skipna=False)["b"]  # 2.0 <- imaginary part gone` and `# 2+3j <- same data, other order`.
PR#68487 reproducer snippet: `df[["b", "a"]].median(skipna=False)["b"]  # 2+3j <- same data, other order`.

oracle_clues: Evidence states `nanmedian`’s `skipna=False` short-circuit returned a bare `np.nan`. The 2-D path uses `np.apply_along_axis`, which takes output dtype from the first slice.
When the column containing the missing value is first, the later complex column output is cast to `float64`, silently discarding the imaginary part.
Concrete oracle from the reproducer: `df.median(skipna=False)["b"]` gives `2.0` while swapping columns to `df[["b","a"]].median(skipna=False)["b"]` gives `2+3j`.

category_specific_evidence: Bug: DataFrame.median with skipna=False discarding the imaginary part of complex columns whose median was well-defined, depending on where the first column holding a missing value sat (:issue:68487).

Commit/bug summary: 2-D nanmedian path builds its result dtype from the first slice; one column holding a missing value cast every later column down to float64, silently discarding the imaginary part of complex columns, depending on where that column sat.

PR#68487 reproducer: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1 + 2j, np.nan], "b": [1 + 2j, 3 + 4j]}); df.median(skipna=False)["b"]  # 2.0  imaginary part gone; df[["b", "a"]].median(skipna=False)["b"]  # 2+3j  same data, other order.

Test in pandas/tests/frame/test_reductions.py: test_median_skipna_false_keeps_complex(na_first) expects df.median(skipna=False) == pd.Series([complex(np.nan), 2 + 3j] if na_first else [2 + 3j, complex(np.nan)], index=list(cols)) where cols contains complex values and np.nan, and also checks df.T.median(axis=1, skipna=False) matches the same expected Series.
reproduction_risks: Column order affects the result for DataFrame.median(skipna=False), because the 2-D path takes output dtype from the first slice; swapping columns changes whether the imaginary part is preserved.

The bug requires skipna=False and at least one column/ slice containing a missing value (np.nan) alongside complex values where the median for the non-missing column has a well-defined imaginary part.
The failure mode is specifically imaginary-part loss (result becomes real, e.g., 2.0 instead of 2+3j) rather than a different numeric magnitude or a different missing-value value.
